sections.content:
The teaching pace is too slow to cover all the originally planned syllabus. Here is the real syllabus covered.

CH1 Introduction
CH2 Vector Space and Metric
CH3 Case Study: K-means algorithm
CH4 Limits and Convergence on Vector Space
CH5 Inner product, Hilbert Spaces, Orthogonality
CH6 Case Study: Kernel Tricks on K-means and Metric Learning
CH7 Linear Functions on Spaces
CH8 Linear Regression and Classifier
CH9 Differentiability of Functions on Vector Spaces, Gradient
CH10 Optimization and Gradient Descent
CH11 Linear Transformation and Operators
CH12 Linear Approximation of Transformation
CH13 Deep Neural Network
CH14 Matrix Differentiation

Overall the course is easy if you have some math background, like MATH 2033 is enough.
The difficulty rose dramatically, around CH12. So be careful.

If you have taken analysis courses harder or equivalent to MATH 2043 (by Ivan),  you will be definitely bored before midterm.

However, there are some highlights in the course, (especially the general approach to differentiation on Banach spaces CH12,13,14) so don't miss them.

All in all, I think the content is not bad and interesting.
sections.teaching:
I would say the biggest problem is the pace of the course. When the content is trivial, she still put a lot of effort proving easy formula, while in my opinion, those are taught in MATH 3322 or easier courses.
I've talked to the professor many times about the pace and the repeating of content. However, she said that there were students can't even catch up even the content is much easier than the past.
I think it's also hard for the instructor to adjust the difficulty of this course.

The other problem is that there are some typos in notes. Some are really wrong and confuse if you didn't attend the lectures.

My advice is Skip every now and then, watch recording when you think the notes are unreadable, and show up sometimes to make sure the content has gone crazy as the last part of the course.
sections.grading:
I think the grading is fair, but it's biased since the content is easy for me.
I get overall 94.8 and get A+.

Sometimes, the professor and TA can't understand quickly, and they will mark your proof wrong. Remember to attend paper checking if you think you are correct.
sections.workload:
The workload is insanely low since it's not easy to design problems for this course.

For each HW, there are about 10 MCs and some "long" questions (in fact they are easy and short).

MCs test your concepts (and your eyes). They are tricky in the sense that some options are wrong in only one notation. So be careful.

Long questions may include some easy proofs, which can be obtained by modifying from lectures.

sections.teaching:
This lecturer had a nice handwritten lecture notes and explained the concepts pretty clear (and it’s too clear that makes the progress lacks behind)

to be honest, the instructor's teaching is still acceptable, but the homework assignments and the exam question are definitely a disaster and should never appeared in 3000 level math course.

There are 40% of the assignments in form of canvas quiz that only allows to hand in once, the assignment quiz questions do not test our understanding to the subject but test how careful we read the qustions. about half of the questions are multiple choice question asking about: what is the correct definition of xxx/wt is the result of xxx appeared in lecture notes, and the wrong choices are just changing one or two minor indexes in the correct definition/result. others are just some direct computations. with no testing on the understanding at all.

secondly, which is the most vital to the students are the question in the two in-tutorial quizzes. each quiz accounts 10% of the course grade and 80 out of 100 marks in the quiz depends on 8 multiple choice question??? these multiple choice questions are similar to assignment quiz (which mean bad). and the remaining 20 marks are: 1. dry run simple clustering algorithm without calculator in first quiz, 2. nearly dictation on a proof provided in lecture notes in second quiz. from these questions I can tell that the instructor didnt spend time and effort in making exam paper at all. And for the final exam paper, there are still 30 points on such multiple choices.

these kind of paper should NOT appear in a high level math course which half of the class are DSCT major that need some in-depth understanding of data analytics tools and I dont think testing out theses shallow multiple choice questions in quiz and assignment could achieve the goal for DSCT students.

it is strongly suggested that the instructor of this course in the future should spend more time in making higher quality exam paper questions rather than giving out simple MCs that accounts a relatively high proportion of course grades.

20% on hw, 20% on two quizzes and 60% on final exam.

Well, I cant really say anything bad about the grading as I got every thing little above uq and I also have some huge deduction on hw (don’t deadline fight guys), but end up with a grade over my expectation (I thing near uq might be a b+).
sections.workload:
As mentioned, the hws are 60% long qs and 40% mc that only allow you to hand in once. All of them are based on lecture notes and if u read through the lecture notes carefully and read every single letter in the mc questions. For long qs, they are also not hard, and some can even find the exact solution in lecture notes.

For preparation of quizzes and final, this is the second time I taken this lecturer’s course (last one is math3322) and I can confirm that u can get nearly full mark if u recite the whole lecture notes and be extremely careful in exam, nothing very hard, just application of the algorithm or the differentiation method taught and sometimes tell u to recite one of the proof in lecture notes. But be reminded that the tolerance of mistakes in this course is VERY LOW, I am too lazy to check out the what if score in canvas but I am sure someone will post it and as far as I know, seems difference in 3-4 marks in total score will end up with a subgrade of difference, so please be extra careful in revising every corner of the lecture notes and be extra careful in exam.

sections.content:
The course content includes different methods and computation techniques on latent vector space. There are some iteration methods that could be the basics of machine learning. Some application examples are provided.

I personally recommend CS students to take this course IFF you have good math background AND you are interested in Machine Learning.

For DSCT student, 3322 and 3332 would be a really good direction for you to think of the FYP project realm no matter you are choosing CS project or MATH project.
sections.teaching:
I think professor CAI is pretty fluent in English and already have a lots of experience in teaching 3322 and 3332.

There are very clear proofs to every lemma and theorem and also some really useful real life application example.
sections.grading:
I think the grading is pretty good.

For the exam, if you could understand each topic well, then you could probably get the answer correctly. But if you don't spend time on understanding all the concept, then probably you would fail to figure the direction of a problem set and be deducted with lots of scores.

So if you make ALL the concepts clear to yourself, then A range is not hard. If you miss one, then it's hard to tell.

(Some people keep asking what would be tested, how the questions would be marked in the exam, blablabla IN A REALLY FLATTERING WAY. Also some people cheat in the quiz. I just want to say you guys are stupid.)
sections.workload:
There is a quiz every three weeks. The quiz is not hard but required to memorize some proofs (which is also useful for the final exam).

As for the homework, it's really light workload I would say.

sections.content:
Basically similar to the previous offering, but we do not cover subdifferential and Fermat’s lemma this semester (maybe this had reduced the difficulty?!).  The course material is self-content if one is familiar with Linear Algebra (like math2121). If one really wants to be well prepared for this course, reading “Linear Algebra Done Right” before the semester start will definitely help since it introduces LA from the vector’s perspective which is what we use in this course.

In each chapter, the professor will talk about some math concepts and then follow by case studies that utilized the concepts learned.  The first few chapters are about how to model a problem (like clustering, regression, classification) to become a minimization problem. The following chapters are about how can we solve the minimization problem (optimization).
sections.teaching: The teaching is great! Prof. Cai has very well-organized notes and explains them clearly. The teaching pace is also easy to follow and Prof. Cai is very responsive to answering questions.
sections.grading:
30% Homeworks (every two weeks)(total 5)

20% Quizzes (every three weeks)(total 3)

50% Final Exam.

The grading for homework, quizzes, and the final are quite lenient this semester, one can get marks as long as the general argument is correct ( don’t need to be as rigorous as some courses like math2033 I believe !?).  

Overall 98.7% is an A, so I believe quite a few people do very well in this course.
sections.workload:
The workload really depends on one’s familiarity with Linear Algebra and the course materials. Most questions in the homework require one to utilize techniques taught in class (like techniques the professor used while proving some theorems). Others can be solved more easily if one knows some properties taught in Linear Algebra courses (like the Orthogonal complement of a subspace). That being said, the professor is very willing to give hints if one asked (which is extremely useful) (Once, he basically taught me how to solve the question).

As for the Quiz, most questions are directly copied from homework. Some proof in the questions requires some special tricks, so make sure one review proof appears in the homework before taking the quiz.

For the Final, the professor will give a sample paper for us to review before the final. Although it is very useful, notice that, unlike the previous year, there are no identical (extremely similar) questions appearing in the actual final this semester.

sections.content:
Content sacrifices depth for breadth in giving a brief introduction into functional analysis and (very brief) convex optimization, as well as some machine learning algos. Boyd and Vanderberghe’s notes are good if you want to get a more holistic understanding of convexity and optimality (eg epigraphs, supporting hyperplane theorem, etc).

Content covered:
1. Norms, vector spaces, k-means, limits and sequences in vector spaces, Banach spaces
2. Inner products, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, Hilbert spaces, kernel methods, ridge/LASSO regression
3. Linear and affine functions, Riesz representation theorem, Frechet derivative, gradient
4. Convexity and optimality: convexity, strict convexity, gradient descent, subgradient and subdifferential, Fermat’s lemma, optimality conditions
Also: Constrained smooth convex optimization, proximity operators, convergence of GD etc was scheduled to be covered but cut due to time constraints.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Cai teaches fairly well and answers questions quickly. He does upload complete lecture notes before class (which he replicates during lectures along with some explanations) so a lot of people do skip. Only gripe is that I prefer typed up notes so I can ctrl+f but his handwriting is very neat and legible, and diagrams are drawn quite nicely too.

Not much to do in tutorials except quizzes and the TA going over HW/quiz answers. Can skip if you got full marks on that HW/quiz, recordings are available anyway.
The TA Jingyang was very helpful during the exam period.
sections.grading:
Homeworks (35%) (6)
Quizzes (30%) (4)
Final (35%) (cumulative)

note: covid semester so quizzes and exams are online

Worth noting that the TA seems to grade light, so mean might be higher than previous semesters.

Homeworks: Usually proofs, some minor calculations. Due date is around one week from time of release. Google/Math Stackexchange is your friend here.
Aggregate mean: 555.6/600, me: 580/600

Quizzes - Usually 3-4 questions, 2-3 being relatively standard. Quiz 3 and 4 had curveball questions that I wasn’t able to prepare for.
Aggregate mean: 345.6/400, me: 375/400

Exam is fairly standard, nothing too special. Like math3322 in previous semester, final is open-book for hard copy notes only. I found the practice final to be very similar to the real thing. Shoutout to Jingyang again for checking my answers on the practice final :p
Mean: 81.8/100, me: 97/100

Important things you need to know:
If you’re aiming for A range, you need to be very familiar with all of convexity and optimality, be able to prove a given function is/is not an inner product/norm, calculate gradient of arbitrary functions, etc. You should also know how to calculate the multivariable subdifferential case and Fermat’s lemma and how to apply it to a problem (eg Find deltaF(x) and find the optimality condition for a global minimizer - that means use Fermat’s lemma.)

My total: 95.90/100 (A)
Idk class mean letter grade but I suspect around B/B-. Maybe a bit higher this semester since on an absolute scale a lot of people did well. I heard from friends that A+ seems to be very difficult to get in this prof's class.
sections.workload:
Varies throughout the semester. I found the first 2 hws to be relatively easy, next 2 to be harder but manageable, last 2 to be a pain in the rear (honestly might have gotten A+ if i didn't mess up hw6). This sem, HW6 was released days before the exam. Other than that, workload is what you want it to be: I revised very little up until the week before the final. If there's a past paper, I highly recommend doing it - the final was extremely similar (the 25pt question almost copied word for word).
Imo, the first big spike in difficulty is the Frechet derivative and gradient calculation, and the second is the calculation of multivariable subdifferentials. If you can get past that, this course is a relative breeze for the beginning 60% of the semester
